text.p: The most significant feature of the government's small business package announced last month was one of the least noticed -- the establishment of a Small Business Innovation Fund to provide capital for small, technology-based firms.
It amounts to the first indication by the Howard government that it is listening to the pleas of industry leaders for the development of a strategic industry policy.

As recently as a month ago Treasurer Peter Costello (Inside Canberra, March 14) was dismissing questions as to what the government's industry policy was by referring to the macro policies of lower interest rates, freeing the labor market, etc.
With the announcement last month of deliberate targeting of small high-tech firms the government has given its first indication that broad economy-wide policies are not sufficient.

One of the major criticisms of this government and the Keating and Hawke governments before it, was that in the area of small business, the small business policy was supposed to fit the needs of the sandwich shop proprietor as well as the young, high tech, high risk company which was aimed at the export market.

The Small Business Innovation Fund (SBIF) is quite a triumph for Industry Minister John Moore, who has been plugging away behind the scenes as almost a sole advocate in Cabinet of the need for targeted industry policies.

All investment decisions taken under SBIF would be taken by the private sector fund managers with the government matching private sector capital raised on a A$2 for every A$1 of private capital raised.
The amount of money is not huge -- A$200 million of government money over four to five years, but at least it is a start.
The other point about the SBIF announcement is it implies some recognition of the importance of innovation in product development.

The coalition's economic policy has always had a major focus on industry input costs -- wages, waterfront reform, transport reform and the like. Important as these things are, they are not the final determinate of industry policy success.
As Employment Minister Senator Amanda Vanstone wrote in an industry paper she produced when in opposition -- if Australia has to match Chinese wages then we've had it.
What has been missing from government policy is a policy towards industry output as well as input. And in output, innovation is all important.

Germany and Japan both have lousy domestic micro economies -- far worse than Australia's -- yet they can afford to carry this load (albeit with increasing difficulty) because they produce superb products based on high-tech innovation for which the world will pay a high price.
